fixtures.name: weak_linkedin_post
fixtures.genre: LinkedIn post announcing a job change

criteria.name: Engagement-inviting close
criteria.description: The final line opens a door for the reader — an invitation to connect, reach out, or engage around the new role — rather than closing with a generic 'excited for what's next' sentiment.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM drafts of job-change LinkedIn posts typically end with generic enthusiasm ("excited for what's next"), so an explicit targeted invitation to engage is a distinctive user preference.

criteria.name: Brevity and restraint
criteria.description: Posts stay short and uncluttered — a single tight paragraph rather than a multi-section essay. The user accepts concise drafts without asking for expansion, accomplishment lists, or added emotional flourish.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM drafts of LinkedIn job-change posts typically include multi-paragraph structure, emoji, hashtag chains, and achievement lists — this criterion explicitly rejects those defaults.

criteria.name: Clean announcement arc
criteria.description: The post moves through a predictable arc — brief acknowledgment of the previous role/tenure, clear statement of the new role, quick thanks to the prior team, and a forward-looking beat — without dwelling on any one section.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
GENERIC
This arc (past role → new role → thanks → forward look) is the standard structure any competent LLM would produce for a LinkedIn job-change announcement by default.

rubric_raw.user_goals_summary: The user wants concise, restrained LinkedIn announcements that acknowledge the past role briefly, state the new role clearly, and close with a forward-looking hook that invites connection rather than generic enthusiasm. They lean toward short, clean posts without heavy embellishment.

rubric.name: Engagement-inviting close
rubric.description: The final line opens a door for the reader — an invitation to connect, reach out, or engage around the new role — rather than closing with a generic 'excited for what's next' sentiment.

dimensions.label: Closing line explicitly invites readers to reach out, connect, or engage
Signals who the invitation is for (e.g., people interested in a specific topic, stage, or role type)
Does not end on a vague enthusiasm line like 'can't wait to share more' as the final beat
The invitation is relevant to the new role or what the user will be working on

rubric.name: Brevity and restraint
rubric.description: Posts stay short and uncluttered — a single tight paragraph rather than a multi-section essay. The user accepts concise drafts without asking for expansion, accomplishment lists, or added emotional flourish.

dimensions.label: Post is one compact paragraph (no multi-section structure or long lists)
Does not enumerate past achievements or projects in detail
Emotional language is warm but understated (avoids superlatives stacked on superlatives)
Avoids hashtag chains, emoji clutter, or LinkedIn-cliché formatting

rubric.name: Clean announcement arc
rubric.description: The post moves through a predictable arc — brief acknowledgment of the previous role/tenure, clear statement of the new role, quick thanks to the prior team, and a forward-looking beat — without dwelling on any one section.

dimensions.label: Opens with a brief nod to the previous role and tenure
States the new role and company clearly and early
Includes a short thank-you to the previous team without extended tribute
Ends with a forward-looking beat rather than looking backward

rubric_raw.coaching_notes: Evidence base is thin — this rubric is a starting draft and should be refined as more announcement posts are written. The strongest signal so far is the user's preference for endings that invite engagement over generic 'excited for what's next' closes. When in doubt, err toward shorter and more restrained rather than adding flourish or detail.

criteria.name: Compactness over completeness
criteria.description: The recap stays tight and resists the pull to add task lists, owners, or deadlines unless asked. When in doubt, the user prefers less over more.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically produce meeting recaps with action items, owners, deadlines, and context paragraphs; explicitly suppressing these and enforcing tight length is a distinctive user preference.

criteria.name: Labeled-bullet structure
criteria.description: Key takeaways are presented as short bullets prefixed with a category label (e.g., 'Decision:', 'Next step:') rather than as prose or unlabeled lists.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically produce recap emails with generic bullets or prose under headers like "Discussion" and "Action Items," not inline category-labeled bullets like "Decision:" / "Next step:" prefixes.

criteria.name: Light close with room for correction
criteria.description: The email ends with a brief, low-pressure invitation for teammates to flag anything missing, rather than a formal summary or call to action.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically end recap emails with explicit next steps, action items, or formal calls to action; a deliberately low-pressure "flag anything missing" close with no homework is a distinctive user preference.

rubric_raw.user_goals_summary: The user wants meeting recaps to be short, scannable summaries that capture decisions and next steps without expanding into task lists or action-item tracking. They prefer a labeled-bullet structure and a light invitation for corrections over elaborate formatting or ownership detail.

rubric.name: Compactness over completeness
rubric.description: The recap stays tight and resists the pull to add task lists, owners, or deadlines unless asked. When in doubt, the user prefers less over more.

dimensions.label: Does not append an action-item/task list unless the user requested one
Avoids adding owners, due dates, or RACI-style detail not raised in the meeting
Body stays under roughly 6 bullets / ~100 words
Opens with a single brief framing line rather than a paragraph of context

rubric.name: Labeled-bullet structure
rubric.description: Key takeaways are presented as short bullets prefixed with a category label (e.g., 'Decision:', 'Next step:') rather than as prose or unlabeled lists.

dimensions.label: Uses a bulleted list for the core content
Bullets are prefixed with short category labels like Priorities / Decision / Next step
Covers the three beats typical of this user's recaps: what was discussed, what was decided, and what happens next
Each bullet expresses a single idea in one line

rubric.name: Light close with room for correction
rubric.description: The email ends with a brief, low-pressure invitation for teammates to flag anything missing, rather than a formal summary or call to action.

dimensions.label: Includes a short line like 'Let me know if I missed anything'
Avoids assigning follow-up homework or a hard call to action
Uses a simple sign-off (e.g., 'Thanks,') rather than elaborate closing language

rubric_raw.coaching_notes: This user treats recaps as lightweight confirmations, not project artifacts — when offered expansions (task lists, owners, timelines), they decline. Default to the shortest version that still captures discussion + decision + next step, and let teammates fill in gaps via the 'let me know if I missed anything' line. Evidence is thin (two-message acceptance), so treat these preferences as a starting hypothesis to refine.

fixtures.name: weak_product_blurb
fixtures.genre: short product description for a landing page

criteria.name: Concrete, quantified hook
criteria.description: Opening line leads with a specific outcome or number (e.g., time saved, bugs caught) rather than an abstract verb phrase like 'automate X'. The user chose a '90% less time' opener over a generic 'Automate your test coverage' opener.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically open product descriptions with abstract capability verbs like "Automate" or "Streamline"; requiring a quantified outcome hook is a distinctive preference.

criteria.name: Technical credibility signals
criteria.description: Blurb names concrete technical integration points (e.g., CI pipeline, no-config setup) so an engineering audience sees it as credible rather than marketing fluff.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM product blurbs tend toward marketing language; explicitly requiring concrete integration points, setup-effort phrasing, and credibility markers targeted at engineers is a distinctive preference.

criteria.name: Tight, scannable length
criteria.description: Blurb stays to roughly 2–3 sentences and ends with a short action-oriented line. Every sentence earns its place; no throat-clearing.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
GENERIC
A competent LLM asked for a short landing page product description would typically produce 2-3 tight sentences ending with a call-to-action by default.

rubric_raw.user_goals_summary: The user wants short, punchy product blurbs for a developer-focused AI tool's landing page. They lean toward concrete, quantified claims over abstract value statements, and expect technical integration details to be surfaced so engineers take the product seriously.

rubric.name: Concrete, quantified hook
rubric.description: Opening line leads with a specific outcome or number (e.g., time saved, bugs caught) rather than an abstract verb phrase like 'automate X'. The user chose a '90% less time' opener over a generic 'Automate your test coverage' opener.

dimensions.label: First sentence contains a specific number, percentage, or measurable outcome
Hook names a user-facing result, not just a product capability
Does not open with a generic imperative like 'Automate...', 'Streamline...', 'Transform...'

rubric.name: Technical credibility signals
rubric.description: Blurb names concrete technical integration points (e.g., CI pipeline, no-config setup) so an engineering audience sees it as credible rather than marketing fluff.

dimensions.label: Mentions how the product fits into an existing developer workflow or toolchain
Addresses setup effort (e.g., 'no config', 'in minutes', 'works with existing X')
Includes customer names, usage stats, or other concrete credibility markers where appropriate

rubric.name: Tight, scannable length
rubric.description: Blurb stays to roughly 2–3 sentences and ends with a short action-oriented line. Every sentence earns its place; no throat-clearing.

dimensions.label: Total length is roughly 2–3 sentences (or under ~50 words)
Ends with a short CTA or concrete next-step line
No sentence is purely decorative — each carries a distinct claim or signal

rubric_raw.coaching_notes: Evidence is thin — the user approved quickly with minimal feedback, so these criteria are a starting hypothesis, not confirmed preferences. When the user says 'pick one,' they want a decisive choice with a one-line rationale, not another round of options. Probe on future drafts to confirm whether they truly prefer quantified hooks or whether that was just one acceptable option.

fixtures.name: weak_birthday_card
fixtures.genre: birthday card message for a coworker

criteria.name: Brevity over personalization
criteria.description: Notes stay short and generic rather than reaching for personal details. When offered the chance to personalize, the user declines — brief is the target, not a compromise.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically try to personalize birthday messages and often expand to warmer, multi-threaded notes; explicitly keeping it short and generic is a distinctive user preference.

criteria.name: Coworker-appropriate distance
criteria.description: Tone reflects a colleague you work with but aren't close to — warm enough to feel sincere, but not claiming friendship or intimacy that isn't there.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
GENERIC
A competent LLM writing a coworker birthday card would already default to warm-but-professional tone, avoid intimate language, and use conventional well-wishes.

rubric_raw.writing_type: short workplace birthday notes for acquaintance-level coworkers
rubric_raw.user_goals_summary: The user wants quick, low-effort birthday notes for coworkers they know only through work. They favor brevity and standard warmth over personalization, and treat these notes as a courtesy rather than a creative exercise.

rubric.name: Brevity over personalization
rubric.description: Notes stay short and generic rather than reaching for personal details. When offered the chance to personalize, the user declines — brief is the target, not a compromise.

dimensions.label: Body of the note is no more than 2–3 short sentences
Avoids inventing or reaching for personal anecdotes, inside jokes, or specifics about the recipient
Conveys one core message (birthday wishes + light workplace acknowledgment) without additional threads

rubric.name: Coworker-appropriate distance
rubric.description: Tone reflects a colleague you work with but aren't close to — warm enough to feel sincere, but not claiming friendship or intimacy that isn't there.

dimensions.label: Avoids language implying friendship or personal closeness (e.g., 'miss you,' 'love,' 'dear friend')
Includes a brief nod to the working relationship (e.g., 'pleasure working with you')
Uses conventional birthday well-wishes rather than emotionally loaded language

rubric_raw.coaching_notes: This user treats coworker birthday notes as a quick courtesy — default to short and generic, and don't pitch personalization options unless asked. When in doubt, shorter wins. Evidence base is thin (one brief exchange); revisit confidence after more examples.

fixtures.name: weak_bug_report
fixtures.genre: internal bug report in a ticket tracker

criteria.name: Minimal field set
criteria.description: Bug reports stick to the core fields (title, summary, repro, expected/actual, severity, env) and avoid optional decorations like screenshot placeholders, tags, or priority labels unless asked. The user treats extras as noise.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically pad bug reports with extras like priority labels, tags, screenshot placeholders, and speculative "possible cause" sections; restricting to a minimal field set is a distinctive preference.

criteria.name: Impact-anchored severity
criteria.description: Severity is stated with a short justification tied to concrete user impact (e.g. 'blocks checkout'), not an unexplained label.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically output severity as a standalone label (e.g., "Severity: High") without tying it to concrete user impact, so requiring an impact-anchored justification is a distinctive preference.

criteria.name: Tight, reproducible steps
criteria.description: Repro steps are short, numbered, and contain only the actions needed to trigger the bug — no narrative framing or extraneous setup.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs often include narrative framing and extra context in repro steps; requiring terse action-only numbered steps with environment split out is a distinctive stylistic discipline.

rubric_raw.user_goals_summary: The user wants concise, no-frills bug reports that include only the essential structured fields. They prefer severity justified by concrete user impact and resist adding optional metadata (screenshots, tags, priority labels) unless explicitly needed.

rubric.name: Minimal field set
rubric.description: Bug reports stick to the core fields (title, summary, repro, expected/actual, severity, env) and avoid optional decorations like screenshot placeholders, tags, or priority labels unless asked. The user treats extras as noise.

dimensions.label: Contains the core fields: title, summary, steps to reproduce, expected, actual, severity, environment
Omits optional metadata fields (screenshot placeholders, tags, priority labels, assignees) unless explicitly requested
Does not add speculative sections like 'possible cause', 'workarounds', or 'notes' without evidence

rubric.name: Impact-anchored severity
rubric.description: Severity is stated with a short justification tied to concrete user impact (e.g. 'blocks checkout'), not an unexplained label.

dimensions.label: A severity level is explicitly stated
Severity is accompanied by a brief reason describing user or business impact
Avoids arbitrary priority scores or labels not grounded in observed impact

rubric.name: Tight, reproducible steps
rubric.description: Repro steps are short, numbered, and contain only the actions needed to trigger the bug — no narrative framing or extraneous setup.

dimensions.label: Steps are numbered and presented as discrete actions
No extraneous setup steps beyond what is needed to reproduce
Environment (browser, OS, version) is specified separately rather than embedded in prose

rubric_raw.coaching_notes: User wants bug reports to stop at 'enough' — resist suggesting screenshots, tags, or priority fields unless asked. Justify severity with a short user-impact phrase rather than an unexplained label. Favor terse, scannable structure; a single 'Good' is their signal that the draft is done.
